chapters.title: Chapter 5: Analysing Performance Like a Manager

lessons.title: Budgets vs Actuals: Reading Variance Reports and MIS Without Getting Lost

children.text: The monthly MIS pack lands in your inbox on the seventh working day. Forty-seven rows, a column of red and green arrows, and a line at the bottom reading "Unfavourable variance ₹61.5 lakh". In the review meeting, three managers explain the three biggest red numbers. None of them explains why the quarter actually went wrong.

Variance analysis is not about listing what moved. It is about separating the causes, in order of size, so the discussion lands on the two or three things that matter. This lesson shows you how to do that with arithmetic a manager can run in ten minutes.

body.text: A variance report is useless until it is split by cause. Selling more at a lower price and selling the same at a higher cost look identical on the bottom line and need completely different responses.

children.text: MIS Is Not the Annual Report
Management information is internal, monthly and unaudited. It exists to support decisions, not to satisfy a regulator, and it obeys different rules.

columns.label: Statutory statements
points: Prepared under Ind AS and Schedule III
Audited annually, filed with MCA and the exchanges
Whole company, or by reportable segment
Accurate and late, arriving weeks after year end

columns.label: Management information (MIS)
points: By department, plant, region, product or customer
Approximate and fast, arriving within days of month end

body.text: The two must still reconcile. If MIS revenue for the year does not tie to statutory revenue, someone is counting differently, usually on discounts, GST, intercompany sales or the cut-off date. Ask for the reconciliation once a quarter. It is the single most useful question a non-finance manager can ask about MIS.

children.text: The Quarter at Kesari Foods
Here is one quarter against budget. Read it the way most people do, then watch what the split reveals.

body.caption: Kesari Foods: quarterly budget against actual (₹ crore)

children.text: The headline reads well. Volumes beat budget by 8% and revenue came in ahead. Yet EBITDA missed by about 31%. Everything needed to explain that is already in the table, and none of it is visible until the variances are split by cause.

children.text: Kesari budgets a variable cost of ₹26 a pack, so budgeted contribution is ₹24. Now split the ₹61.5 lakh miss.

body.text: The quarter was not a volume problem or a cost problem. It was a discount that bought volume at a loss: ₹67.5 lakh of price given away to win ₹48 lakh of contribution. A report that simply flagged "material cost overrun, ₹79 lakh unfavourable" would have sent the meeting after the wrong culprit entirely.

body.title: Split the revenue variance
body.prompt: A distributor budgeted 40,000 units at ₹250 each and actually sold 44,000 units at ₹240. What is the price variance, in ₹? Enter it as a positive number for the amount lost.
body.explanation: Price variance = (₹240 minus ₹250) × 44,000 units = minus ₹4,40,000. The volume variance is +4,000 units × ₹250 = ₹10,00,000 at budget price, so revenue is still ₹5,60,000 ahead of budget. Revenue grew and every unit earned ₹10 less.

children.text: Flex the Budget Before You Judge a Cost

The most common error in Indian MIS packs is comparing actual costs at actual volume against budgeted costs at budgeted volume. If you sold 8% more, your material cost should be higher. Judging it against the original budget punishes the plant for the sales team's success.

body.title: The flexed budget, step by step

children.text: A flexed budget restates the budget at actual volume, so variable costs are compared like with like.
Original budget:
₹6.50 crore of material for 25 lakh packs, which is ₹26 a pack.
Flex it to actual volume:
27 lakh packs × ₹26 = ₹7.02 crore. This is what the material should have cost.
Compare with actual:
₹7.29 crore actual against ₹7.02 crore flexed, which is an overspend of ₹27 lakh.
Split the raw variance:
the total ₹79 lakh gap is ₹52 lakh caused by higher volume, which is expected and fine, and ₹27 lakh of genuine overspending, which needs explaining.
Only the ₹27 lakh belongs to procurement and production. Report the raw ₹79 lakh without flexing and you will spend the meeting arguing about a number that was never a problem.

body.title: Which figure should the plant answer for?
body.question: Budgeted material cost was ₹6.50 crore for 25 lakh packs. Actual was ₹7.29 crore for 27 lakh packs. What is the genuine spending overrun the plant should explain?
options: ₹79 lakh, the full gap against budget
₹27 lakh, the gap against the budget flexed to 27 lakh packs
₹52 lakh, the part caused by higher volume
Nothing, because revenue also beat budget
body.explanation: Flexing the budget to actual volume gives ₹7.02 crore. The overspend against that is ₹27 lakh. The remaining ₹52 lakh is simply the cost of making more packs, which the extra sales paid for.

body.title: Name the direction
body.textWithBlank: A cost that comes in higher than budget is described in a variance report as an ___ variance.
body.explanation: Favourable and unfavourable describe the effect on profit, not whether the number rose or fell. Higher revenue is favourable, higher cost is unfavourable, and Indian MIS packs often use the word adverse for the same thing.

children.text: Writing Commentary That Survives the Meeting
Most variance commentary is a restatement of the number in words: "Other expenses were ₹10 lakh above budget due to higher expenses." Useless. A usable line has four parts.
Cause:
what actually happened, specifically. Not "higher freight" but "diesel up 9% and two extra Nagpur trips after a machine breakdown".
Impact:
the rupee effect and whether it repeats. A one-off breakdown is not the same as a permanent rate increase.
Action:
what is being done, with a name attached.
Date:
when the fix lands, so the next pack can check it.

body.caption: Two ways to write the same variance

cells: Material cost unfavourable by ₹79 lakh due to higher costs.

Material ₹27 lakh above the flexed budget. Palm oil rates rose 6% from January and were not passed through. Recurring, about ₹9 lakh a month at current volumes. Procurement to close a three-month forward contract by 20 April, and pricing to review the pack price for May.
Revenue favourable, volumes ahead of plan.

Revenue ₹33 lakh ahead, but only because volume was 8% above plan. Realisation was ₹2.50 a pack below budget after festive discounting, costing ₹67.5 lakh. Discount scheme ends 15 April and will not be extended.

body.title: Your MIS commentary is due tomorrow
body.scenario: You head the western region for Kesari Foods. Your region carried most of the discount that caused the ₹67.5 lakh price variance, and you also delivered the volume beat. The CEO has asked every regional head for a one-page note before the quarterly review.
body.prompt: What goes in your note, and what do you propose?
body.modelAnswer:
Open with the split, not the defence:
1. Region delivered 8% volume growth, worth about ₹48 lakh of contribution at budgeted economics.
2. The discount that drove it cost ₹67.5 lakh across all packs sold, so the net effect on EBITDA was negative ₹19.5 lakh. State this plainly before anyone else does.
Then explain why the discount happened:
3. What triggered it: a competitor scheme, a distributor demand, a festive window or a stock clearance decision, and who approved it.
4. Whether the discount was targeted or blanket. A blanket cut applies to volume that would have sold anyway, which is what makes the price variance so much larger than the volume gain.
Then what changes:
5. Discounts move to targeted schemes: specific packs, specific weeks, specific accounts, with a cap on total give-away per quarter expressed in rupees, not in percentage.
6. Ask for approval thresholds: any discount above a set percentage needs sign-off, since the arithmetic shows a 5% price cut needs roughly a 12% volume rise just to hold contribution at a 48% margin.
7. Commit to reporting realisation per pack every month alongside volume, so price erosion is visible early rather than at quarter end.
And what you want from others:
8. Pricing support on the pass-through of palm oil costs, since holding price while input costs rise is a second, separate squeeze.
9. A view from supply chain on whether the extra 2 lakh packs created any inventory or freight cost that has not yet been reported.

body.title: Fix your own MIS pack
steps: Count the metrics in your current pack. If there are more than about ten on page one, propose a shorter version.
Check whether cost variances are flexed to actual volume. If not, ask for it.
Ask for revenue variance split into price and volume, at least for the top three products.
Confirm the MIS reconciles to the statutory numbers at least annually, and find the last reconciliation.
Rewrite your last three commentary lines with cause, impact, action and date.
Agree a materiality threshold with finance, for example anything above 5% or ₹5 lakh, so small variances stop consuming meeting time.

cards.definition: Internal management information: unaudited, frequent and organised by department or product rather than by statute.
The difference between actual and budget, described as favourable or unfavourable by its effect on profit.
The profit effect of selling more or fewer units than planned, valued at budgeted contribution.
The profit effect of realising a different price than planned, across actual volume sold.
The budget restated at actual volume, so variable cost performance is compared like with like.
A presentation walking from budgeted profit to actual profit, one cause at a time.
The actual average price received per unit after discounts and schemes.
A forecast updated each month or quarter, used alongside a fixed annual budget.

points: MIS is internal, fast and approximate. Statutory statements are external, slow and audited. They must still reconcile.
A total variance is meaningless until split by cause, because opposite problems produce the same bottom line.
Volume variance values extra units at budgeted contribution. Price variance applies the price gap to everything sold.
Always flex the budget to actual volume before judging a variable cost, or you will blame the plant for the sales team's success.
A discount applies to all volume, not just the incremental volume, which is why price variances are usually larger than they look.
Commentary needs cause, impact, action and a date. Anything less is the number restated in words.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the distributor example are fictional, with figures constructed for teaching. Variance conventions differ between companies, so confirm how your own MIS defines realisation, contribution and flexed budgets before comparing across teams.
